entries.clue: Medic’s poor score with Guardian crossword debut (7,7)

indicatorNotes.poor: poor means in bad shape, so the letters are knocked out of order
indicatorNotes.debut: a debut is a first appearance, so only the first letter of crossword is taken

annotation.surface: A doctor makes a miserable showing on their first attempt at the Guardian crossword.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's after Medic reads as 'Medic is', joining definition to wordplay. The Guardian is where this puzzle appeared, so the surface is a wink at the paper itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Category: a cardiac surgeon is a doctor who operates on the heart.

entries.clue: Express unhappiness about programme that’s trashy (6)

indicatorNotes.about: about means surrounding, so CRY goes round APP

blocks.note: to cry is to express unhappiness
an app is a computer programme

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling about a television show they think is rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Programme' suggests television, but here it is a software application, shortened to APP.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: crappy is slang for poor quality, as trashy is.

entries.clue: Awfully sorry to have pocketed a chaplet (6)

indicatorNotes.Awfully: awfully means badly, so the letters of sorry are done badly, jumbled
indicatorNotes.to have pocketed: to pocket is to put inside, so the jumbled letters take A inside them

annotation.surface: An apology for having slipped a wreath of flowers into one's pocket.
annotation.walkthrough: Chaplet has two senses, a wreath for the head and a string of prayer beads; the answer uses the second.
annotation.definitionFit: Exact term: a chaplet is a short string of prayer beads, a form of rosary.

entries.clue: Poorly writer’s in favour of vague reply (10)

indicatorNotes.vague: vague means not clearly formed, so the letters of reply lose their shape and are rearranged

blocks.note: the writer is the setter, who would say I'm (I am)
pro means for, in favour of

annotation.surface: An ailing author says they support giving a noncommittal answer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poorly' looks like a description of the writer's health, but it is the definition. The writer is the setter, so writer's is I'M.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to do something improperly is to do it poorly, badly.

entries.clue: Clue for March: one in seven desperately trying to make friends and influence people (5,9)

annotation.definition: trying to make friends and influence people
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a verb phrase; the answer is a noun for such a campaign

indicatorNotes.in: in places one letter inside the others
indicatorNotes.desperately: desperately means wildly, so the letters of seven are thrown about

blocks.note: 'CHARM off' would be a clue for MARCH, with off telling the solver to rearrange CHARM

annotation.surface: A cryptic instruction followed by a picture of someone straining to be liked.
annotation.walkthrough: The first piece is a reverse clue: you must imagine a clue whose answer is MARCH. CHARM with the anagram indicator OFF does that job.
annotation.definitionFit: Exact term: a charm offensive is a deliberate campaign of friendliness to win people over.

entries.clue: See 1
Replace McEnroe in broadcast? (9)

indicatorNotes.in broadcast: something in a broadcast is heard rather than read, so the answer is taken from its sound

blocks.note: John McEnroe was a top-seeded tennis player, a super seed; the ? marks him as an example

annotation.surface: A suggestion that a commentator take John McEnroe's place on air.
annotation.walkthrough: McEnroe is really a tennis champion who became a TV commentator, so 'broadcast' fits the surface while doing a sound job. A seed is a ranked player in a tournament draw.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to supersede something is to take its place, to replace it.

entries.clue: Almost raw and red (4)

indicatorNotes.Almost: almost means not quite all, so each word loses its last letter

blocks.note: RED with its last letter removed too, since 'Almost' governs both

annotation.surface: A description of a steak barely cooked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Almost' applies to both words: each is cut short. Read whole, the clue also describes a rare steak.
annotation.definitionFit: Exact term: rare meat is cooked only briefly, so it is almost raw and red inside.

entries.clue: Not going to a restaurant with inane git misbehaving (6,2)

indicatorNotes.misbehaving: misbehaving means acting badly, so the letters do not stay in line

annotation.surface: Staying home instead of dining out because a silly idiot is causing trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: A git is British slang for an unpleasant or foolish person.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain description: eating in means having a meal at home rather than going out to eat.

entries.clue: Wedding band for a shilling in Northern poor regions (4,4)

indicatorNotes.poor: poor means in bad shape, so the letters of regions are jumbled

annotation.surface: A wedding ring bought for a shilling, a pre-decimal British coin, in a deprived part of the north.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition comes from Edward Lear's poem The Owl and the Pussycat, where the Piggy-wig sells the ring at the end of his nose for one shilling so the owl and cat can marry.
annotation.definitionFit: Literary allusion: in Lear's poem the pig's nose ring is bought for a shilling and used as the wedding ring.

entries.clue: A model turned storyteller (5)

indicatorNotes.turned: turned means turned round, so POSE is read backwards

annotation.surface: A fashion model who changed careers to become a writer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: to model is to pose.
annotation.definitionFit: Example: Aesop was the ancient Greek teller of fables.

entries.clue: Being criminals sucks (9)

blocks.note: as = being, as in 'as it was raining'

annotation.surface: A blunt verdict that a life of crime is no fun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sucks' looks like slang for 'is bad', but it is the definition: to aspirate is to draw in by suction.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: aspirate means to suck or draw in, as when fluid is drawn out with a syringe.

entries.clue: Each prior show to begin with cast (10)

indicatorNotes.to begin with: to begin with means at the start, so only the first letter of show is taken

blocks.note: per = each, as in £5 per head

annotation.surface: Each earlier production had its own cast from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show' and 'cast' both suggest theatre, but show gives only its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the cast of a production is the set of performers in it.

entries.clue: Single move divorce city’s backing (4)

indicatorNotes.backing: backing means going backwards, so RENO is read in reverse

blocks.note: Reno, Nevada was famous for quick divorces

annotation.surface: A newly single person moving to a city that supports divorce.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Single move' reads as a person moving house after a breakup, but it is the definition. The 's reads as 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a oner is something done in a single go, one unbroken stroke or move.

entries.clue: Pianist playing ‘Waterfalls’ (4,6)

indicatorNotes.playing: playing means moving about freely, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A pianist performing a piece called Waterfalls.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make Waterfalls look like a song title, fitting the picture of a pianist playing it.
annotation.definitionFit: Example: Fats Waller was an American jazz pianist and songwriter.

entries.clue: Old individual helping to get acquittal (11)

blocks.note: a ration is a portion, a helping

annotation.surface: An elderly person assisting in securing someone's acquittal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Helping' reads as assisting, but it is the noun: a helping of food, a ration.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: exoneration is being cleared of blame, as an acquittal clears the accused.

entries.clue: See 4
Is in France consuming load – this? (8)

annotation.definition: Is in France consuming load – this?

indicatorNotes.in France: in France means the French word is needed, so 'is' becomes EST
indicatorNotes.consuming: consuming means taking in, so EST takes CARGO inside it

annotation.surface: A question about what a person in France is busy eating.
annotation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue asks what is eaten in France: an escargot, a snail. The dash and question mark mark it as the thing being consumed.
annotation.definitionFit: Exact term: escargot is the French word for a snail eaten as food.

entries.clue: Massive waste in fossil fuel (8)

annotation.surface: A complaint about enormous wastage in the fossil fuel industry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Massive' sits so naturally before 'waste' that it looks like an adjective in the surface, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: colossal means huge, massive.

entries.clue: They possibly pilfer hot stores, removing content (11)

annotation.definition: They possibly pilfer hot stores, removing content

indicatorNotes.possibly: possibly means in some possible arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.removing content: content is what a thing contains, so stores loses its inside, leaving S…S

blocks.note: STORES with its middle letters taken out

annotation.surface: People who might steal stolen goods from shops, emptying them.
annotation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes what shoplifters do: pilfer from stores and take their contents. Hot means stolen, which adds to the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain description: shoplifters steal goods from shops, removing their contents.

entries.clue: Criticism oddly not heard for Figaro? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Figaro is an example of a barber, hence the ?

indicatorNotes.oddly not: oddly not means the odd-numbered letters are not kept, so only the even ones remain

blocks.note: a barb is a cutting remark

annotation.surface: A question about whether a critic was deaf to Figaro.
annotation.walkthrough: Figaro is the hero of Rossini's opera The Barber of Seville.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Figaro, hero of Rossini's opera, is a Seville hairdresser who shaves his customers.

entries.clue: On board boat, ten days – be there! (6)

indicatorNotes.On board: on board means inside the vessel, so the answer is found inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the word breaks, from the end of boat to the start of days

annotation.surface: An invitation to a ten-day trip on a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' fits the boat so neatly that it hides its job of pointing inside the next words.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to attend is to be there, present.

entries.clue: Feel reasonably well or berserk (4)

blocks.note: as in 'How do you feel?' 'I am…'

annotation.surface: Someone asked how they are, and whether they are fine or going mad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I am OK' is how one says one feels reasonably well; drop the I and the phrase runs together.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to run amok is to go berserk, wild.

entries.clue: Nasty and perhaps guilty, wearing fake suntan (10)

indicatorNotes.wearing: wearing means having on the outside, so the jumbled letters go round PLEA
indicatorNotes.fake: fake means not genuine, so suntan is not in its true order

blocks.note: guilty is one plea in court; perhaps marks it as an example

annotation.surface: A nasty character, probably guilty, sporting a fake tan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guilty' looks like a description of the nasty person, but it stands for a plea entered in court.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: unpleasant means nasty.

entries.clue: Go straight (5)

blocks.note: go in the sense of run off quickly, in British slang
straight in the sense of honest, within the law

annotation.surface: An instruction to an offender to give up crime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go straight' reads as one phrase meaning reform, but it splits in two: to LEG IT is British slang for to run away, and LEGIT is short for legitimate.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: leg it means to go quickly, and legit means straight, above board.

entries.clue: Cocktail – one drunk by a clubber dancing (4,5)

indicatorNotes.drunk by: what is drunk is taken in, so I goes inside the jumbled letters
indicatorNotes.dancing: dancing means moving about, so the letters of a clubber are rearranged

annotation.surface: A cocktail sipped by someone on the dance floor at a club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like it describes the drink, but it tells you one letter is swallowed inside the others.
annotation.definitionFit: Example: a Cuba libre is a cocktail of rum, cola and lime.

entries.clue: Teaching the students at last, mathematician is using body language (9)

indicatorNotes.at last: at last means at the end, so each word gives its final letter

blocks.note: last letters of teachinG thE studentS

annotation.surface: A mathematics lecturer finally getting through to students by waving their hands about.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one teacher's lesson, but the first three words only supply their last letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: gesturing is communicating with movements of the hands or body.

entries.clue: See 24 Down
Farm work up to maturity (7)

blocks.note: to come of age is to reach maturity

annotation.surface: Working on a farm until one comes of age.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up to maturity' reads as one phrase, but till and age are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain description: tillage is preparing and cultivating land for crops.

entries.clue: Look embarrassed seeing nurse regularly in motion (4,3)

indicatorNotes.regularly: regularly means at regular intervals, so every other letter of nurse is kept

blocks.note: a motion is a bowel movement, and a turd is what it produces

annotation.surface: Someone blushing when a nurse keeps appearing during their movements.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Motion' suggests movement, but it is the medical sense, a bowel motion, which explains why the nurse would cause embarrassment.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain description: to turn red is to blush, the look of someone embarrassed.
